Chapter 1. Setting Out on a Journey Through Time and Faith.
You ever feel that restless urge—not just to see a place, but to peel back its layers, to really get at the memories and beliefs that have shaped it? That’s where this journey starts. It’s about letting curiosity guide you, about wanting to trace the footsteps of people who walked these lands centuries ago. The Eastern Mediterranean is a world where ancient hills meet bustling cities, and every stone, every whisper of prayer, carries stories reaching all the way back to the first days of Christianity. Here, the past isn’t something you leave behind—it’s right there, woven into daily life, lingering in traditions older than most countries.
What inspired this journey? It all goes back to John Moschos, a monk from the sixth century who roamed these same lands, hungry for wisdom, gathering stories from Christian monasteries scattered across the vast Byzantine world. Sure, a lot’s changed since then, but you can still feel the echo of Moschos’s pilgrimage. The path winds through Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, and Egypt—places where Christian communities have managed to survive, often against incredible odds, sometimes overshadowed by empires, conquests, and shifting faiths.
The first steps take us to Mount Athos, that legendary peninsula in northern Greece. For over a thousand years, it’s been a haven for Orthodox monks. Imagine the air thick with incense, the steady hum of chanting, life moving to the rhythm of ancient ritual. Monks in black robes glide quietly through the halls, their faces marked by years of devotion. Out there, the world is noisy and distracting, but inside these monastery walls, time seems to slow right down. The concerns of modern life? They just fade into the background.
Picture a sunlit courtyard one morning—a visitor sits with an elderly monk. The monk’s hands are rough from a lifetime of work, and his eyes have this gentle sadness to them. He talks about the challenges facing Christian communities beyond Athos—about monasteries that once thrived, now standing empty, their walls slowly crumbling. He remembers when pilgrims came from all over, searching for guidance and comfort. These days, he says, so many of these places are forgotten, their stories at risk of disappearing.
As the journey heads east, the scenery changes. The green forests of Greece give way to Anatolia’s dry hills, where the remains of ancient churches stand silent, witnesses to a world that’s mostly vanished. In a little village, a caretaker sweeps a church that hasn’t seen a congregation in years. Lighting a candle, he quietly defies the slow erosion of his community. He shares memories of his childhood—the village alive with festivals and processions. Now, most of his neighbors have moved on, searching for work or safety.
You start to see that the story of Christianity in the Middle East isn’t just about faith—it’s about survival. These communities have weathered centuries of upheaval: wars, invasions, the rise and fall of empires. Every generation has faced its own set of challenges, learning to adapt to new rulers and shifting borders. And yet, there’s a thread of continuity. The prayers, the rituals, the stories passed down from parent to child—they’ve kept these communities alive, even as their numbers shrink.
Traveling through these lands, you can’t help but notice the resilience of those who remain. In one monastery perched on a rocky outcrop, a group of nuns tends a garden, their laughter ringing through the courtyard. They talk about hope, about the importance of holding tight to their traditions, even as the world outside keeps changing. For them, faith isn’t just a belief—it’s a way of living, a thread tying them to their ancestors, and to each other.
So, this journey isn’t just about looking back. It’s about understanding what it means to belong to a community that’s both ancient and fragile. The people you meet along the way—they’re not relics of history. They’re living proof that faith can endure, even when faced with uncertainty and loss. Their stories remind us: some things, no matter how much the world changes, have the power to last.
